dublinCore.title: Signal Operations: Shift, Scale and Reverse
creator: Dan McCreary
subject: Signal operations
Time shifting
Time scaling
Time reversal
Elementary signals
Decimation and expansion
dublinCore.description: Interactive MicroSim that transforms an elementary signal x(t) into y(t) = A x(a(t - t0)) and tracks three landmark points from x to y (t_y = t_x/a + t0). It can overlay the common shift-before-scale mistake z(t) = A x(at - t0), which shifts by t0/a, and switch to discrete time to show decimation x[Mn] discarding samples and expansion x[n/L] inserting zeros.
relation: Chapter 2: Introduction to Signals and Systems

learningObjectives: Calculate where a point of x(t) at time t_x appears in y(t) = A x(a(t - t0)), using t_y = t_x/a + t0
Distinguish x(a(t - t0)) from x(at - t0) and calculate the actual shift t0/a produced by the second form
Predict the effect of a < 0 (reversal), |a| > 1 (compression), |a| < 1 (stretching) and A on a signal's shape and position
Explain why decimation x[Mn] loses samples and why expansion x[n/L] needs inserted zeros or interpolation
Calculate the area of a time-scaled impulse using delta(at) = delta(t)/|a|

misconceptions.misconception: x(at - t0) is x(at) delayed by t0
misconceptions.correction: x(at - t0) = x(a(t - t0/a)), so the delay is t0/a; the correct form is x(a(t - t0))
misconceptions.evidence: Check 'Show the common mistake': with a = 2 and t0 = 2 s the red z(t) lands 1 s to the left of the blue y(t), and with a = -1 it moves the opposite way

misconceptions.misconception: x[n/2] stretches a sequence just as x(t/2) stretches a waveform
misconceptions.correction: x[n/2] is undefined at odd n; zeros are inserted there and interpolation is needed to fill them, while samples discarded by x[2n] cannot be recovered
misconceptions.evidence: In DT mode set a = 1/2 to see hollow inserted-zero circles, and a = 2 or 4 to see crossed-out samples of x that never reach y

accessibility.screenReaderScript: Two stacked plots on the same time axis: the original signal x(t) in gray and the transformed signal y(t) = A x(a(t - t0)) in blue. Three colored landmark points P, Q and R are joined by dashed lines from x to y, and a table lists their times. Sliders set the shift t0, the scale a and the amplitude A; checkboxes reverse time, overlay the common shift-before-scale mistake in red, and switch to discrete time.

controls.label: Shift t0
controls.description: Sets the time shift t0 in seconds; in DT mode it moves in whole samples (n0)

controls.label: Scale a
controls.description: Sets the magnitude of the time-scale factor a; in DT mode it steps through 1/4, 1/3, 1/2, 1, 2, 3, 4

controls.label: Amplitude A
controls.description: Sets the amplitude scale factor A; negative values flip the signal upside down

controls.label: Discrete time (DT)
controls.description: Switches to stem plots on integer n with integer shifts and scale factors M or 1/L

controls.label: Reverse time
controls.description: Replaces a with -a, flipping the signal about t = 0 before the shift

controls.label: Show the common mistake
controls.description: Overlays z(t) = A x(at - t0) in red and explains that it shifts by t0/a, not t0

visualElements.description: Upper plot: the original signal x(t) or x[n] in gray with landmarks P, Q, R
Lower plot: y(t) = A x(a(t - t0)) in blue, optional mistake z(t) in red, landmark connectors from the upper plot
Formula read-out, order-of-operations or mistake explanation, and a landmark table t_x -> t_y = t_x/a + t0 (and t_z)

model.description: Evaluates y(t) = A x(a(t - t0)) and z(t) = A x(at - t0) for an elementary signal and maps landmark times with t_y = t_x/a + t0 and t_z = (t_x + t0)/a; in discrete time y[n] = A x[a(n - n0)] is defined only where a(n - n0) is an integer, otherwise a zero is inserted
equations: z(t) = A x(at - t0) = A x(a(t - t0/a))
y[n] = x[n/L] if L divides n, else 0 (expansion)

instructionalStrategies: Predict landmark positions before reading the table
Contrast the correct and mistaken transformation side by side
extensions: Add a second stage so students can compose two operations and compare the result with a single combined operation
